claim: Biological aging is the gradual, progressive decline in system integrity that occurs with advancing chronological age, causing morbidity and disability.
source: Biological aging is the gradual, progressive decline in system integrity that occurs with advancing chronological age, causing morbidity and disability.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that draws on established scientific understanding of aging processes.

claim: Aging of the global population is producing forecasts of rising burden of disease and disability.
source: Aging of the global population is producing forecasts of rising burden of disease and disability (Harper, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harper, 2014.

claim: Treatments for single diseases will not address the burden challenge arising from multiple age-related diseases.
source: Because this burden arises from multiple age-related diseases, treatments for single diseases will not address the burden challenge (Goldman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goldman et al., 2013.

claim: Treatments to slow aging itself could prevent or delay multiple diseases that increase with advancing age.
source: Geroscience research suggests an appealing alternative: treatments to slow aging itself could prevent or delay the multiple diseases that increase with advancing age, perhaps with a single therapeutic approach (Gladyshev, 2016; Kaeberlein, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gladyshev, 2016 and Kaeberlein, 2013.

claim: Aging arises from an accumulation of cellular-level changes that increase vulnerability to diseases affecting many different organ systems.
source: This deterioration is thought to arise from an accumulation of cellular-level changes. These changes, in turn, increase vulnerability to diseases affecting many different organ systems (Kennedy et al., 2014; López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kennedy et al., 2014 and López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: Animal studies suggest treatments that slow the accumulation of cellular-level changes can extend healthy lifespan.
source: Animal studies suggest treatments that slow the accumulation of cellular-level changes can extend healthy lifespan (Campisi et al., 2019; Kaeberlein et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campisi et al., 2019 and Kaeberlein et al., 2015.

claim: Human trials of aging treatments are challenging because humans live much longer than model animals.
source: However, human trials of these treatments are challenging because humans live much longer than model animals, making it time-consuming and costly to follow up human trial participants to test treatment effects on healthy lifespan.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the difference in lifespan between humans and model organisms.

claim: The National Advisory Council on Aging approved development of healthspan-extension trials involving young and midlife adults.
source: Involving young and midlife adults in healthspan-extension trials has been approved for development by the National Advisory Council on Aging (2019 CTAP report to NACA).
evidence: Supported by citation to 2019 CTAP report to NACA.

claim: Traditional endpoints such as disease diagnosis or death are too far in the future to serve as outcomes in midlife trials of treatments to slow aging.
source: In midlife trials of treatments to slow aging, called geroprotectors (Moskalev et al., 2016), traditional endpoints such as disease diagnosis or death are too far in the future to serve as outcomes.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the long time horizon for disease development in midlife adults.

claim: Measures that quantify the pace of deterioration in biological system integrity could be used as surrogate endpoints for healthy lifespan extension.
source: Translation of geroprotector treatments to humans could be aided by measures that quantify the pace of deterioration in biological system integrity in human aging. Such measures could be used as surrogate endpoints for healthy lifespan extension (Justice et al., 2016; Justice et al., 2018; Moskalev et al., 2016), even with young-to-midlife adult trial participants.
evidence: Supported by citations to Justice et al., 2016; Justice et al., 2018; Moskalev et al., 2016.

claim: Blood DNA methylation is a biological substrate highly sensitive to changes in chronological age.
source: Recent efforts to develop such measures have focused on blood DNA methylation as a biological substrate highly sensitive to changes in chronological age (Fahy et al., 2019; Horvath and Raj, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fahy et al., 2019 and Horvath and Raj, 2018.

claim: Methylation-clock algorithms confound methylation patterns arising from early-life exposures with methylation patterns related to biological aging during adulthood.
source: However, a limitation is that individuals born in different years have grown up under different historical conditions (Schaie, 1967). For example, people born 70 years ago experienced more exposure to childhood diseases, tobacco smoke, airborne lead, and less exposure to antibiotics and other medications, and lower quality nutrition, all of which leave signatures on DNA methylation (Bell et al., 2019). As a result, the clocks confound methylation patterns arising from early-life exposures to methylation-altering factors with methylation patterns related to biological aging during adulthood.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schaie, 1967 and Bell et al., 2019, and logical inference about cohort effects.

claim: The Dunedin Study collected a panel of 18 blood-chemistry and organ-system-function biomarkers at three successive waves when Study members were aged 26, 32, and 38 years.
source: In Step 1, which we previously reported (Belsky et al., 2015), we collected a panel of 18 blood-chemistry and organ-system-function biomarkers at three successive waves of the Dunedin Study, which follows a 1972–73 population-representative one-year birth cohort (N = 1037). We used repeated-measures data collected when Study members were aged 26, 32, and 38 years old to quantify rates of biological change.
evidence: This describes the data collection procedure in the Dunedin Study, supported by citation to Belsky et al., 2015.

claim: Pace of Aging was normally distributed and showed marked variation among Study members who were all the same chronological age.
source: Pace of Aging was normally distributed, and showed marked variation among Study members who were all the same chronological age, confirming that individual differences in biological aging do emerge already by age 38, years before chronic disease onset.
evidence: This is a finding from the Dunedin Study data analysis.

claim: Study members with faster Pace of Aging performed more poorly on tests of physical function, showed signs of cognitive decline, were rated as looking older, and reported themselves to be in worse health.
source: As compared to other Study members who were the same chronological age but had slower Pace of Aging, Study members with faster Pace of Aging performed more poorly on tests of physical function; showed signs of cognitive decline on a panel of dementia-relevant neuropsychological tests from an early-life baseline; were rated as looking older based on facial photographs; and reported themselves to be in worse health (Belsky et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Belsky et al., 2015.

claim: Faster Pace of Aging is associated with early-life factors important for aging: familial longevity, low childhood social class, and adverse childhood experiences.
source: Subsequently, we reported that faster Pace of Aging is associated with early-life factors important for aging: familial longevity, low childhood social class, and adverse childhood experiences (Belsky et al., 2017), and that faster Pace of Aging is associated with older scores on Brain Age, a machine-learning-derived measure of structural MRI differences characteristic of different age groups (Elliott et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Belsky et al., 2017 and Elliott et al., 2019.

claim: Pace of Aging was not well-correlated with published epigenetic age clocks.
source: Notably, Pace of Aging was not well-correlated with published epigenetic age clocks, which were designed to measure how old a person is rather than how fast they are aging biologically (Belsky et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Belsky et al., 2018b.

claim: Elastic-net regression was applied to derive a DNA-methylation predictor of Pace-of-Aging called DunedinPoAm.
source: Elastic-net regression was used to develop a DNA-methylation predictor of Pace-of-Aging, called DunedinPoAm for Dunedin(P)ace(o)f(A)ging(m)ethylation.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used to develop DunedinPoAm.

claim: DunedinPoAm is qualitatively different from previously published DNA methylation measures of aging that were developed by comparing older individuals to younger ones.
source: DunedinPoAm is qualitatively different from previously published DNA methylation measures of aging that were developed by comparing older individuals to younger ones. Those measures, often referred to as 'clocks,' are state measures. They estimate how much aging has occurred in an individual up to the point of measurement. DunedinPoAm is a rate measure.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction made by the authors based on the different methodological approaches.

claim: DunedinPoAm is designed to function as a speedometer, recording how fast the subject is aging.
source: Rather than a clock that records how much time has passed, DunedinPoAm is designed to function as a speedometer, recording how fast the subject is aging.
evidence: This is a conceptual description of what DunedinPoAm is intended to measure.

claim: The elastic-net-derived DunedinPoAm algorithm selected a set of 46 CpG sites.
source: This analysis selected a set of 46 CpG sites (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is a result from the elastic-net regression analysis.

claim: The 46-CpG DunedinPoAm algorithm was associated with the longitudinal 26–38 Pace of Aging measure with a Pearson r = 0.56.
source: The 46-CpG elastic-net-derived DunedinPoAm algorithm, applied in the age-38 Dunedin DNA methylation data, was associated with the longitudinal 26–38 Pace of Aging measure (Pearson r = 0.56, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Dunedin Study analysis, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bootstrap-cross-validation analysis estimated the out-of-sample correlation between DunedinPoAm and Pace of Aging to be r = 0.33.
source: This is likely an overestimate of the true out-of-sample correlation because the analysis is based on the same data used to develop the DunedinPoAm algorithm; bootstrap-cross-validation analysis estimated the out-of-sample correlation to be r = 0.33 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from bootstrap cross-validation analysis, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Study members with faster DunedinPoAm at age 38 performed more poorly at age 45 on tests of balance, walking speed, chair stands, and motor coordination, and reported more functional limitations.
source: Study members with faster DunedinPoAm at age 38 performed more poorly at age 45 on all physical performance tests, with the exception of grip strength, and reported more functional limitations (standardized effect-sizes for tests of balance, walking speed, chair stands, and physical limitations r = 0.15–0.29, p<0.001 for all; grip strength r = 0.05, 95% CI [−0.02–0.12], p=0.162).
evidence: This is a prospective association finding from the Dunedin Study.

claim: Study members with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm experienced greater decline in balance at age 45.
source: Study members with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm experienced greater decline in balance at age 45 (r = 0.11 [0.04–0.19], p=0.008) and a greater increase in physical limitations (r = 0.10 [0.02–0.18], p=0.012).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of change scores in the Dunedin Study.

claim: Study members with faster DunedinPoAm at age 38 performed more poorly on all age-45 cognitive tests.
source: Study members with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm performed more poorly on all age-45 cognitive tests (r = 0.14–0.28, p<0.001 for all).
evidence: This is a finding from the Dunedin Study analysis.

claim: On average, Study members showed a decline of 2.00 IQ points across the follow-up interval from childhood to age 45.
source: On average, Study members showed a decline of 2.00 IQ points (95% CI [1.31–2.70]) across the follow-up interval.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the Dunedin Study.

claim: Study members with faster DunedinPoAm experienced more cognitive decline from childhood to age 45.
source: Both analyses found that Study members with faster DunedinPoAm experienced more decline (difference-score r = 0.12, [0.05–0.19], p=0.001; residualized change r = 0.20 [0.13–0.27]).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of cognitive decline in the Dunedin Study.

claim: Study members with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm rated themselves to be in worse health at age 45.
source: Study members with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm rated themselves to be in worse health at age 45 (r = 0.27, 95% CI [0.20–0.34]).
evidence: This is a finding from the Dunedin Study analysis.

claim: Study members with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm were rated as looking older at age 45.
source: These Study members were also rated as looking older (r = 0.35 [0.28–0.43]).
evidence: This is a finding from the Dunedin Study analysis of facial aging.

claim: Those with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm were more likely to transition to fair/poor health categories by age 45.
source: Those with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm were more likely to transition to the fair/poor categories (Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR) = 1.79 95% CI [1.48–2.18]).
evidence: This is a finding from the Dunedin Study analysis.

claim: Study members with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm were rated as looking older relative to peers at age 45 than they had been at age 38.
source: Study members with faster age-38 DunedinPoAm were rated as looking older relative to peers at age 45 than they had been at age 38 (r = 0.10 [0.03–0.18]).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of change in facial aging in the Dunedin Study.

claim: DunedinPoAm effect-sizes were similar to and sometimes larger than effect-sizes for the original Pace of Aging measure across domains of physical function, cognitive function, and subjective signs of aging.
source: Across the domains of physical function, cognitive function, and subjective signs of aging, DunedinPoAm effect-sizes were similar to and sometimes larger than effect-sizes for the original Pace of Aging measure (Supplementary file 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the Dunedin Study analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the Understanding Society sample, the mean DunedinPoAm was 1.03 years of biological aging per each calendar year.
source: In this mixed-age sample, the mean DunedinPoAm was 1.03 years of biological aging per each calendar year (SD = 0.07).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the Understanding Society Study analysis.

claim: Understanding Society participants who were of older chronological age tended to have faster DunedinPoAm.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, Understanding Society participants who were of older chronological age tended to have faster DunedinPoAm (r = 0.11, [0.06–0.17], p<0.001; Figure 3 Panel A).
evidence: This is a finding from the Understanding Society Study analysis, shown in Figure 3 Panel A.

claim: The Horvath, Hannum, and Levine epigenetic clocks were highly correlated with chronological age in the Understanding Society sample.
source: These epigenetic clocks were highly correlated with chronological age in the Understanding Society sample (Horvath Clock r = 0.91, Hannum Clock r = 0.92, Levine Clock r = 0.88).
evidence: This is a finding from the Understanding Society Study analysis.

claim: DunedinPoAm was moderately correlated with epigenetic age acceleration measured from the clocks proposed by Hannum (r = 0.24) and Levine (r = 0.30).
source: Nevertheless, DunedinPoAm was moderately correlated with epigenetic age acceleration measured from the clocks proposed by Hannum (r = 0.24) and Levine (r = 0.30).
evidence: This is a finding from the Understanding Society Study analysis.

claim: DunedinPoAm was less-well correlated with acceleration measured from the Horvath clock (r = 0.06).
source: DunedinPoAm was less-well correlated with acceleration measured from the Horvath clock (r = 0.06).
evidence: This is a finding from the Understanding Society Study analysis.

claim: Understanding Society participants with faster DunedinPoAm had more advanced KDM Biological Age.
source: Participants with faster DunedinPoAm had more advanced KDM Biological Age (r = 0.20 95% CI [0.15–0.26], p<0.001;) and worse self-rated health (r = −0.22 [-0.28,–0.16], p<0.001;).
evidence: This is a finding from the Understanding Society Study analysis.

claim: During follow-up from 1999 to 2013, 46% of NAS participants died over a mean follow-up of 7 years.
source: During follow-up from 1999 to 2013, 46% of NAS participants died over a mean follow-up of 7 years (SD = 7).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the NAS analysis.

claim: NAS participants with faster DunedinPoAm at baseline were at increased risk of death.
source: Those with faster DunedinPoAm at baseline were at increased risk of death (Hazard Ratio (HR) = 1.29 [1.16–1.45], p<0.001; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the NAS analysis, shown in Figure 4.

claim: During NAS follow-up, n = 175 participants were diagnosed with a new chronic disease.
source: During follow-up across 4 assessments during 1999–2013 (n = 1448 observations of the N = 771 participants), n = 175 NAS participants were diagnosed with a new chronic disease.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the NAS analysis.

claim: NAS participants with faster baseline DunedinPoAm were at increased risk of new chronic disease diagnosis.
source: Those with faster baseline DunedinPoAm were at increased risk of new diagnosis (HR = 1.19 [1.03–1.38], p<0.019).
evidence: This is a finding from the NAS analysis.

claim: In repeated-measures analysis of prevalent chronic disease, faster DunedinPoAm was associated with having a higher level of chronic disease morbidity in NAS.
source: In repeated-measures analysis of prevalent chronic disease, faster DunedinPoAm was associated with having a higher level of chronic disease morbidity (IRR = 1.15 [1.11–1.20], p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from the NAS analysis.

claim: NAS participants' DunedinPoAm values increased across repeated assessments.
source: Consistent with Understanding Society analysis showing faster DunedinPoAm in older as compared to younger adults, NAS participants' DunedinPoAm values increased across repeated assessments. For every five years of follow-up, participants' DunedinPoAms increased by 0.012 (SE = 0.002, p<0.001) units, or about 0.2 standard deviations.
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal analysis in the NAS.

claim: E-Risk adolescents who grew up in lower socioeconomic-status families exhibited faster DunedinPoAm.
source: E-Risk adolescents who grew up in lower socioeconomic-status families exhibited faster DunedinPoAm (Cohen's d for comparison of low to moderate SES = 0.21 [0.06–0.35]; Cohen's d for comparison of low to high SES = 0.44 [0.31–0.56]; Pearson r = 0.19 [0.13–0.24]).
evidence: This is a finding from the E-Risk Study analysis.

claim: E-Risk adolescents with exposure to more types of victimization exhibited faster DunedinPoAm.
source: In parallel, E-Risk adolescents with exposure to more types of victimization exhibited faster DunedinPoAm (Cohen's d for comparison of never victimized to one type of victimization = 0.28 [0.15–0.41]; Cohen's d for comparison of never victimized to two types of victimization = 0.48 [0.23–0.72]; Cohen's d for comparison of never victimized to three or more types of victimization = 0.53 [0.25–0.81]; Pearson r = 0.15 [0.10–0.20]).
evidence: This is a finding from the E-Risk Study analysis.

claim: CALERIE randomized N = 220 adults on a 2:1 ratio to treatment of 25% caloric restriction or control ad-libitum diet for two years.
source: CALERIE randomized N = 220 adults on a 2:1 ratio to treatment of 25% caloric restriction (CR-treatment) or control ad-libitum (AL-control, as usual) diet for two years (Ravussin et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the CALERIE trial design, supported by citation to Ravussin et al., 2015.

claim: CALERIE participants who were randomized to CR-treatment experienced a slower rate of biological aging as compared to participants in the AL-control arm based on longitudinal change analysis of clinical-biomarker data.
source: We previously reported that CALERIE participants who were randomized to CR-treatment experienced a slower rate of biological aging as compared to participants in the AL-control arm based on longitudinal change analysis of clinical-biomarker data from the baseline, 12 month, and 24 month follow-up assessments (Belsky et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Belsky et al., 2018a.

claim: Among CALERIE control participants, the rate of increase in KDM Biological Age was 0.71 years of biological age per 12 month follow-up interval.
source: Among control participants, the rate of increase in biological age measured using the Klemera-Doubal method (KDM) Biological Age algorithm was 0.71 years of biological age per 12 month follow-up interval.
evidence: This is a finding from the CALERIE trial analysis.

claim: Among CALERIE treatment participants, the rate of increase in KDM Biological Age was only 0.11 years of biological age per 12 month follow-up interval.
source: In contrast, among treatment participants, the rate of increase was only 0.11 years of biological age per 12 month follow-up interval (difference b = −0.60 [-0.99,–0.21]).
evidence: This is a finding from the CALERIE trial analysis.

claim: There was no group difference in DunedinPoAm between CR-treatment and AL-control participants at CALERIE baseline.
source: As expected, there was no group difference at baseline (AL M = 1.00, SD = 0.05; CR M = 1.01, SD = 0.06, p-value for difference = 0.440).
evidence: This is a finding from the CALERIE trial analysis.

claim: For CALERIE AL-control participants, faster baseline DunedinPoAm predicted faster biological aging over the 24 month follow-up.
source: For AL-control participants, faster baseline DunedinPoAm predicted faster biological aging over the 24 month follow-up, although in this small group this association was not statistically significant at the alpha = 0.05 level (b = 0.22 [-0.05, 0.49], p=0.104).
evidence: This is a finding from the CALERIE trial analysis.

claim: For CALERIE CR-treatment participants, the association of baseline DunedinPoAm with future rate of aging was sharply reduced.
source: For CR-treatment participants, the association of baseline DunedinPoAm with future rate of aging was sharply reduced, (b = −0.08 [-0.24, 0.09], p=0.351), although the difference between the rate of aging in the AL-control and CR-treatment groups did not reach the alpha = 0.05 threshold for statistical significance (interaction-term testing difference in slopes b = −0.30 [-0.61, 0.01], p-value=0.060).
evidence: This is a finding from the CALERIE trial analysis.

claim: DunedinPoAm captured critical information about Dunedin Study members' healthspan-related characteristics.
source: First, while DunedinPoAm was not a perfect proxy of Pace of Aging, it nevertheless captured critical information about Dunedin Study members' healthspan-related characteristics.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings from the Dunedin Study analysis.

claim: DunedinPoAm showed promise as an easy-to-implement alternative to Pace of Aging.
source: In sum, DunedinPoAm showed promise as an easy-to-implement alternative to Pace of Aging.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the findings.

claim: Age differences in DunedinPoAm parallel population demographic patterns of mortality risk.
source: Age differences in DunedinPoAm parallel population demographic patterns of mortality risk.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Understanding Society and NAS findings.

claim: DunedinPoAm is related to but distinct from alternative approaches to quantification of biological aging.
source: DunedinPoAm is related to but distinct from alternative approaches to quantification of biological aging.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the correlation analyses with other measures.

claim: DunedinPoAm is already variable by young adulthood and is accelerated in young people at risk for eventual shortened healthspan.
source: Third, DunedinPoAm is already variable by young adulthood and is accelerated in young people at risk for eventual shortened healthspan.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the E-Risk Study analysis.

claim: DunedinPoAm analysis of the CALERIE trial provided proof-of-concept for using DunedinPoAm to quantify biological aging in geroprotector intervention studies.
source: Fourth, DunedinPoAm analysis of the CALERIE trial provided proof-of-concept for using DunedinPoAm to quantify biological aging in geroprotector intervention studies.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the CALERIE trial findings.

claim: DunedinPoAm measures the rate of aging over the recent past.
source: DunedinPoAm measures the rate of aging over the recent past.
evidence: This is a conceptual description of what DunedinPoAm is designed to measure.

claim: The relatively modest size of the Dunedin cohort and the lack of other cohorts with requisite repeated biomarkers limited sample size for machine-learning analysis to develop methylation algorithms.
source: The relatively modest size of the Dunedin cohort and the lack of other cohorts that have the requisite three or more waves of repeated biomarkers to measure the Pace of Aging limited sample size for our machine-learning analysis to develop methylation algorithms.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The Dunedin cohort, Understanding Society, NAS, E-Risk cohorts and CALERIE trial sample were mostly of white European descent.
source: The Dunedin cohort in which DunedinPoAm was developed and the Understanding Society, NAS, and E-Risk cohorts and CALERIE trial sample in which it was tested were mostly of white European descent.
evidence: This is a description of the study samples.

claim: Follow-up of DunedinPoAm in more diverse samples is needed to establish cross-population validity.
source: Follow-up of DunedinPoAm in more diverse samples is needed to establish cross-population validity.
evidence: This is a limitation and recommendation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: DunedinPoAm can be implemented in Illumina 450k and EPIC array data.
source: It can be implemented in Illumina 450 k and EPIC array data, making it immediately available for testing in a wide range of existing datasets as a complement to existing methylation measures of aging.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical applicability of DunedinPoAm.

claim: DunedinPoAm offers a unique measurement for intervention trials and natural experiment studies investigating how the rate of aging may be changed.
source: Critically, DunedinPoAm offers a unique measurement for intervention trials and natural experiment studies investigating how the rate of aging may be changed by behavioral or drug therapy, or by environmental modification.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of DunedinPoAm based on the findings.

claim: The Dunedin Study is a longitudinal investigation of health and behavior in a complete birth cohort of N = 1,037 individuals born between April 1972 and March 1973 in Dunedin, New Zealand.
source: The Dunedin Study is a longitudinal investigation of health and behavior in a complete birth cohort. Study members (N = 1,037; 91% of eligible births; 52% male) were all individuals born between April 1972 and March 1973 in Dunedin, New Zealand (NZ), who were eligible based on residence in the province and who participated in the first assessment at age 3.
evidence: This is a description of the Dunedin Study cohort.

claim: The Dunedin cohort represents the full range of socioeconomic status on NZ's South Island and matches the NZ National Health and Nutrition Survey on key health indicators.
source: The cohort represents the full range of socioeconomic status on NZ's South Island and matches the NZ National Health and Nutrition Survey on key health indicators (e.g., BMI, smoking, GP visits) (Poulton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poulton et al., 2015.

claim: The Dunedin cohort is primarily white (93%).
source: The cohort is primarily white (93%) (Poulton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poulton et al., 2015.

claim: At the Dunedin Study age 45 assessment, 94% of the 997 study members still alive took part.
source: Assessments were carried out at birth and ages 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 26, 32, 38 and, most recently, 45 years, when 94% of the 997 study members still alive took part.
evidence: This is a description of the Dunedin Study retention rate.

claim: Understanding Society is an ongoing panel study of the United Kingdom population.
source: Understanding Society is an ongoing panel study of the United Kingdom population (https://www.understandingsociety.ac.uk/).
evidence: This is a description of the Understanding Society Study.

claim: The Normative Aging Study (NAS) is an ongoing longitudinal study on aging established by the US Department of Veterans Affairs in 1963.
source: The Normative Aging Study (NAS) is an ongoing longitudinal study on aging established by the US Department of Veterans Affairs in 1963. Details of the study have been published previously (Bell et al., 1972).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bell et al., 1972.

claim: The NAS is a closed cohort of 2280 male veterans from the Greater Boston area enrolled after an initial health screening to determine that they were free of known chronic medical conditions.
source: Briefly, the NAS is a closed cohort of 2280 male veterans from the Greater Boston area enrolled after an initial health screening to determine that they were free of known chronic medical conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the NAS cohort.

claim: The Environmental Risk (E-Risk) Longitudinal Twin Study tracks the development of a birth cohort of 2,232 British participants.
source: The Environmental Risk (E-Risk) Longitudinal Twin Study tracks the development of a birth cohort of 2,232 British participants.
evidence: This is a description of the E-Risk Study cohort.

claim: The E-Risk sample was drawn from a larger birth register of twins born in England and Wales in 1994–1995.
source: The sample was drawn from a larger birth register of twins born in England and Wales in 1994–1995.
evidence: This is a description of the E-Risk Study sampling.

claim: The E-Risk sample comprised 56% monozygotic (MZ) and 44% dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs.
source: This sample comprised 56% monozygotic (MZ) and 44% dizygotic (DZ) twin pairs; sex was evenly distributed within zygosity (49% male).
evidence: This is a description of the E-Risk Study sample composition.

claim: At the E-Risk age 18 assessment, 93% of the participants took part.
source: Home-visits assessments took place when participants were aged 5, 7, 10, 12 and, most recently, 18 years, when 93% of the participants took part.
evidence: This is a description of the E-Risk Study retention rate.

claim: In the CALERIE trial, participants in the caloric-restriction arm averaged 12% reduction in caloric intake over the course of the trial.
source: Over the course of the trial, participants in the caloric-restriction arm averaged 12% reduction in caloric intake (about half the prescribed reduction).
evidence: This is a finding from the CALERIE trial.

claim: In the CALERIE trial, participants in the ad libitum condition reduced caloric intake by <2%.
source: Participants in the ad libitum condition reduced caloric intake by <2% (Ravussin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ravussin et al., 2015.

claim: DNA methylation was measured from Illumina 450k Arrays in the Dunedin Study, NAS, and E-Risk Study.
source: DNA methylation was measured from Illumina 450 k Arrays in the Dunedin Study, NAS, and E-Risk Study and from Illumina EPIC 850 k Arrays in the Understanding Society study and the CALERIE Trial.
evidence: This describes the DNA methylation measurement methods used in the studies.

claim: DNA was derived from whole blood samples in all studies.
source: DNA was derived from whole blood samples in all studies.
evidence: This describes the biological sample type used for DNA methylation analysis.

claim: None of the 46 CpGs included in the DunedinPoAm algorithm overlapped with CpGs in the Horvath, Hannum, and Levine epigenetic clocks.
source: None of the 46 CpGs included in the DunedinPoAm algorithm overlapped with CpGs in these epigenetic clocks.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of the DunedinPoAm algorithm with other epigenetic clocks.

claim: Pace of Aging was scaled in units representing the mean trend in the cohort, that is the average physiological change occurring during one calendar year.
source: Pace of Aging was scaled in units representing the mean trend in the cohort, that is the average physiological change occurring during one calendar year (N = 954, M = 1, SD = 0.38).
evidence: This describes the scaling of the Pace of Aging measure.

claim: The mPoA algorithms developed across the 100 bootstrap repetitions included different sets of CpGs (range of 21–209 CpGs selected, M = 54, SD = 27 CpGs).
source: The mPoA algorithms developed across the 100 bootstrap repetitions included different sets of CpGs (range of 21–209 CpGs selected, M = 54, SD = 27 CpGs).
evidence: This is a finding from the bootstrap cross-validation analysis.

claim: The mPoA algorithms developed across bootstrap repetitions were highly correlated (mean pairwise r = 0.90, SD = 0.14).
source: However, the resulting algorithms were highly correlated (mean pairwise r = 0.90, SD = 0.14).
